name: Vitamin B12-responsive methylmalonic acidemia type cblB

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Consensus diagnostic criteria for methylmalonic acidemia

criteria.description: Elevated methylmalonic acid levels in plasma or urine
Clinical and biochemical responsiveness to vitamin B12 supplementation
Identification of pathogenic mutations in the MMAB gene
Presence of metabolic acidosis with elevated anion gap
Neurological symptoms such as developmental delay or hypotonia

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of elevated methylmalonic acid with confirmed MMAB gene mutation and documented vitamin B12 responsiveness
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Genetic testing is essential to confirm diagnosis and differentiate from other methylmalonic acidemia types.

pathognomonic.notes: Biochemical hallmark detected in plasma and urine
Improvement of metabolic parameters and symptoms upon B12 supplementation
Pathogenic variants in MMAB gene confirm diagnosis
searchTerms: MMAB gene defect with metabolic symptoms

common.notes: Delayed acquisition of motor and cognitive milestones
Reduced muscle tone commonly observed in infancy
Elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis during metabolic crises
Poor feeding and vomiting in early infancy
Reduced activity and responsiveness during metabolic decompensation

occasional.notes: Occur during metabolic crises or due to neurotoxicity
Poor growth secondary to metabolic instability
Enlarged liver due to metabolic overload
Mild to moderate anemia may be present
Low blood sugar during metabolic crises

rare.notes: Progressive vision loss due to optic nerve damage

laboratory: Markedly elevated methylmalonic acid in plasma and urine
Metabolic acidosis with elevated anion gap
imaging: Brain MRI may show basal ganglia abnormalities during crises
Occasional cerebral atrophy in chronic cases
other: Positive clinical response to high-dose vitamin B12 therapy

distinguishingFeatures: Mutations in MMAA gene instead of MMAB
Different biochemical profile on enzymatic assays
Elevated propionic acid rather than methylmalonic acid

redFlags: Severe metabolic acidosis refractory to standard treatment
Rapid neurological deterioration during metabolic crises
Poor response or worsening despite vitamin B12 supplementation
references: Fowler B, Leonard JV, Baumgartner MR. Causes of and diagnostic approach to methylmalonic acidurias. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2008;31(3):350-360.
Watkins D, Rosenblatt DS. Inherited disorders of vitamin B12 metabolism: a review. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2011;34(1):1-14.
Orphanet Report Series. Vitamin B12-responsive methylmalonic acidemia type cblB. ORPHA:79311.
